Supplementing Recurrent Neural Network Wave Functions with Symmetry and Annealing to Improve Accuracy

Mohamed Hibat-Allah Affiliation:  Vector Institute, MaRS Centre, Toronto, Ontario, M5G 1M1, Canada Affiliation:  Department of Physics and Astronomy, University of Waterloo, Ontario, N2L 3G1, Canada Email: mohamed.hibat.allah@uwaterloo.ca    Roger G. Melko Affiliation:  Department of Physics and Astronomy, University of Waterloo, Ontario, N2L 3G1, Canada Affiliation:  Perimeter Institute for Theoretical Physics, Waterloo, ON N2L 2Y5, Canada    Juan Carrasquilla Affiliation:  Vector Institute, MaRS Centre, Toronto, Ontario, M5G 1M1, Canada Affiliation:  Department of Physics and Astronomy, University of Waterloo, Ontario, N2L 3G1, Canada
Abstract

Recurrent neural networks (RNNs) are a class of neural networks that have emerged from the paradigm of artificial intelligence and has enabled lots of interesting advances in the field of natural language processing. Interestingly, these architectures were shown to be powerful ansatze to approximate the ground state of quantum systems [1]. Here, we build over the results of Ref. [1] and construct a more powerful RNN wave function ansatz in two dimensions. We use symmetry and annealing to obtain accurate estimates of ground state energies of the two-dimensional (2D) Heisenberg model, on the square lattice and on the triangular lattice. We show that our method is superior to Density Matrix Renormalisation Group (DMRG) for system sizes larger than or equal to 14×1414\times 14 on the triangular lattice.

   

1 Introduction

In recent years, deep learning has proven useful in quantum many-body physics [2, 3, 4, 5]. Namely in tasks such as quantum state tomography [6, 7] and finding ground states of quantum many-body Hamiltonians [8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 1, 14]. Yet, up to now, the numerical study of frustrated quantum systems remains challenging due to the debilitating sign problem [15, 16].

Interestingly, recurrent neural networks (RNNs) [17, 18, 19] have shown a significant advantage in the study of quantum systems [7, 1, 14, 20, 21]. In this paper, we aim to show the potential of RNNs in the study of frustrated quantum systems that suffer from the sign problem [15, 16]. To do this, we focus on the prototypical Heisenberg model and show that by applying symmetries and annealing leads to accurate representations of the ground state. In Sec. 2, we describe our improved RNN architecture and annealing scheme. In Sec. 3, we show results for the Heisenberg model on the square and the triangular lattices. We demonstrate that our method is superior compared to the Density Matrix Renomalization Group (DMRG) [22, 23] on system sizes larger than 14×1414\times 14 up to 16×1616\times 16.

2 Methods

2.1 Recurrent neural network wave functions

To model a complex-valued wave function |Ψ⟩\ket{\Psi}, we use the following decomposition

Ψ𝜽​(𝝈)=p𝜽​(𝝈)​exp⁡(i​ϕ𝜽​(𝝈)),\Psi_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{\sigma})=\sqrt{p_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{\sigma})}\exp(\text{i}\phi_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{\sigma})),

where 𝜽\bm{\theta} denotes the variational parameters of the ansatz wave function |Ψ𝜽⟩\ket{\Psi_{\bm{\theta}}}, and 𝝈=(σ1,σ2,…,σN)\bm{\sigma}=(\sigma_{1},\sigma_{2},\ldots,\sigma_{N}) is a spin configuration. In our paper, we use a complex RNN (cRNN) wave function to handle states that change sign in the computational basis [1]. A key feature of RNN wave functions is the ability to obtain uncorrelated samples to estimate observables through autoregressive sampling [1, 24]. More details about this sampling procedure in 1D and 2D can be found in Refs. [1, 25].

In order to efficiently encode 2D correlations, we use a two-dimensional recursion relation as follows [25]:

𝒉i,j=F⁡([𝝈i−1,j;𝝈i,j−1]​T​[𝒉i−1,j;𝒉i,j−1]+𝒃).\bm{h}_{i,j}=F\!\left([\bm{\sigma}_{i-1,j};\bm{\sigma}_{i,j-1}]T[\bm{h}_{i-1,j};\bm{h}_{i,j-1}]+\bm{b}\right). (1)

𝒉i,j\bm{h}_{i,j} is a hidden state with two indices for each spin in the 2D lattice. The symbol [.;.][.;.] denotes concatenation operation of two vectors, while 𝝈i,j\bm{\sigma}_{i,j} is the one-hot encoding of the spin σi,j\sigma_{i,j}. The tuneable arrays TT and 𝒃\bm{b} are a tensor and bias vector, respectively. Since 𝒉i,j\bm{h}_{i,j} can be considered as a summary of the history of spins that were previously generated, it is used to compute the conditional probabilities and conditional phases as follows:

p𝜽​(σi,j|σ<i,j)\displaystyle p_{\bm{\theta}}(\sigma_{i,j}|\sigma_{<i,j}) =Softmax​(U​𝒉i,j+𝒄)⋅𝝈i,j,\displaystyle=\text{Softmax}(U\bm{h}_{i,j}+\bm{c})\cdot\bm{\sigma}_{i,j}, (2)
ϕ𝜽​(σi,j|σ<i,j)\displaystyle\phi_{\bm{\theta}}(\sigma_{i,j}|\sigma_{<i,j}) =π​Softsign​(V​𝒉i,j+𝒅)⋅𝝈i,j.\displaystyle=\pi\ \text{Softsign}(V\bm{h}_{i,j}+\bm{d})\cdot\bm{\sigma}_{i,j}. (3)

Here σ<i,j\sigma_{<i,j} stands for the spins that were previously generated on the zigzag path as shown in Fig. 1(a). U,VU,V and 𝒄,𝒅\bm{c},\bm{d} are additional variational parameters. From the two previous relations, the probability p𝜽​(𝝈)p_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{\sigma}) and the phase ϕ𝜽​(𝝈)\phi_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{\sigma}) can be computed respectively by taking the product (resp. sum) of p𝜽​(σi,j|σ<i,j)p_{\bm{\theta}}(\sigma_{i,j}|\sigma_{<i,j}) (resp. ϕ𝜽​(σi,j|σ<i,j)\phi_{\bm{\theta}}(\sigma_{i,j}|\sigma_{<i,j})).

We note that to compute 𝒉i,j\bm{h}_{i,j} in the recursion relation (1), we use the neighbouring hidden states and spins, as demonstrated in Fig. 1(a). We also remark that a tensorized operation of the hidden states and the spins is chosen instead of a concatenation operation (see Eq. (1)) to improve the expressivity of the 2D RNN as shown in Ref. [25]. In this paper, we also use a gated version of the 2D RNN to further improve the accuracy of our 2D cRNN wave function ansatz. More details are shown in Appendix. A.

Furthermore, symmetries in a system of interest can be incorporated in RNN wave functions, namely U⁡(1)U(1) symmetry and discrete lattice symmetries as it was shown in Ref. [1]. We highlight that adding symmetries significantly improves the accuracy of a variational calculation, as motivated in the literature with the example of RBM wave functions [26]. We finally emphasize that the variational parameters 𝜽\bm{\theta} are optimized with the variational Monte Carlo (VMC) scheme to minimize E𝜽=⟨Ψ𝜽|​H^​|Ψ𝜽⟩E_{\bm{\theta}}=\bra{\Psi_{\bm{\theta}}}\hat{H}\ket{\Psi_{\bm{\theta}}} where H^\hat{H} is the Hamiltonian describing a quantum system of interest. More details about this scheme can be found in the Appendix of Ref. [1].

2.2 Variational Annealing

Finding the ground state of a non-stoquastic Hamiltonian is limited by the sign problem [15, 16], and has shown to induce rugged landscapes during the VMC optimization [27]. The latter can make our ansatz stuck in a local minima, similarly to what is commonly observed in spin glass models at low temperatures. We take inspiration from the concept of annealing, where we supplement VMC with an artificial temperature to overcome local minima during a VMC optimization. This procedure has been already explored in Ref. [25] for the purpose of finding ground states of spin-glass models. Here, we explore this idea in the context of finding ground states of frustrated quantum systems.

In order to supplement the VMC scheme with annealing, we add a pseudo-entropy [14] on top of variational energy E𝜽E_{\bm{\theta}} to obtain a variational free energy:

F𝜽​(n)=E𝜽−T⁡(n)​Sclassical​(p𝜽),F_{\bm{\theta}}(n)=E_{\bm{\theta}}-T(n)S_{\rm classical}(p_{\bm{\theta}}), (4)

where SclassicalS_{\rm classical} is the von Neumann entropy, given by

Sclassical(p𝜽)=−∑𝝈p𝜽(𝝈)log(p𝜽(𝝈)).S_{\rm classical}(p_{\bm{\theta}})=-\sum_{\bm{\sigma}}p_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{\sigma})\log\left(p_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{\sigma})\right). (5)

Here the sum goes over all possible configurations {𝝈}\{\bm{\sigma}\}. In this case T⁡(n)T(n) is a pseudo-temperature. The latter is annealed starting from some initial temperature T0T_{0} to zero temperature as follows: T⁡(n)=T0​(1−n/Nannealing)T(n)=T_{0}(1-n/N_{\rm annealing}) where n∈[0,Nannealing]n\in[0,N_{\rm annealing}] and NannealingN_{\rm annealing} is the total number of annealing steps.

In our setup, we follow the same scheme in Ref. [25], where we first do NwarmupN_{\rm warmup} training steps to prepare our RNN wave function close to the minimum of F𝜽​(n=0)F_{\bm{\theta}}(n=0). In the second step, we keep the parameters of our ansatz fixed and we change nn to n+1n+1. In step 3, we perform NtrainN_{\rm train} gradient steps to bring the RNN ansatz closer to the minimum of F𝜽​(n+1)F_{\bm{\theta}}(n+1). After iterating over steps 2 and 3, we arrive at n=Nannealingn=N_{\rm annealing}. At this point, we perform a user-defined number of gradient steps NconvergenceN_{\rm convergence} to further improve our estimate of the ground state energy of H^\hat{H}. A flowchart detailing this procedure is provided in Fig. 1(b).

3 Results

We focus our attention on the task of finding the ground state of the two dimensional anti-ferromagnetic Heisenberg model on the square lattice and on the triangular lattice with open boundary conditions (OBC). The Hamiltonian is given as follows:

H^=14​∑⟨i,j⟩(σ^ix​σ^jx+σ^iy​σ^jy+σ^iz​σ^jz),\hat{H}=\frac{1}{4}\sum_{\langle i,j\rangle}(\hat{\sigma}_{i}^{x}\hat{\sigma}_{j}^{x}+\hat{\sigma}_{i}^{y}\hat{\sigma}_{j}^{y}+\hat{\sigma}_{i}^{z}\hat{\sigma}_{j}^{z}),

where the sum is over nearest neighbours and σ^ix,y,z\hat{\sigma}_{i}^{x,y,z} are Pauli matrices. In the square lattice case, H^\hat{H} has a C4​vC_{4v} symmetry11 1 A point group with four rotations and four mirror reflections (vertical, horizontal and diagonal)., whereas for the case of the triangular lattice, H^\hat{H} has a C2​dC_{2d} symmetry22 2 A point group with two rotations and two diagonal mirror reflections.. We also remark that in both cases, the ground state has zero magnetization [28], due to the U⁡(1)U(1) symmetry of the Hamiltonian H^\hat{H}. We show that enforcing these symmetries in our ansatz allows to obtain a better accuracy without adding more parameters. More details about how to apply symmetries to the 2D cRNN ansatz can be found in the Appendix of Ref. [1].

3.1 Heisenberg model on the square lattice

Since the Hamiltonian H^\hat{H} can be made stoquastic on the sqaure lattice [29, 30], we set T0=0T_{0}=0, i.e., we do not use annealing in this case. The latter choice is motivated by the observations shown in Appendix. B.

First, we train our 2D cRNN wave function to find the ground state of the 6×66\times 6 square lattice with and without applying the symmetries of the Hamiltonian H^\hat{H}. We find in Fig. 2(a) that increasing the number of symmetries encoded in the cRNN leads to a more accurate estimation of the ground state energy.

We also use our 2D cRNN wave function to estimate the ground state of the 10×1010\times 10 square lattice after applying U⁡(1)U(1) and C4​vC_{4v} symmetries. The results are shown in Fig. 2(b), where we compare our estimates with projected-pair entangled states (PEPS) [31], Pixel CNN wave functions [13], as well as Quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) [31]. These results show that our ansatz is more accurate compared to PEPS and PixelCNN. We also find that QMC is the best among all the three methods.

3.2 Heisenberg model on the triangular lattice

Due to the frustrated, non-bipartite nature of the triangular lattice, the Hamiltonian H^\hat{H} can no longer be made stoquastic with a simple unitary transformation. Such a Hamiltonian can make the VMC optimization landscape rough and filled with local minima [27]. Here, we use annealing to overcome local minima and to obtain accurate estimates of ground state energies.

To demonstrate the idea of annealing, we target the ground state of the 4×44\times 4 triangular lattice at different number of annealing steps NannealingN_{\rm annealing}. The results in Fig. 3(a) show that starting from a non-zero T0T_{0} allows to obtain a lower value of the relative error as opposed to traditional VMC where the initial pseudo-temperature T0=0T_{0}=0. We also remark that a higher accuracy is obtained by increasing the number of annealing steps, which underlines the importance of adiabaticity in our scheme.

We now focus our attention on larger system sizes. Here we train our 2D cRNN wave function using annealing for a system size 6×66\times 6. We then optimize our ansatz at larger system sizes after increasing the lattice side length by 22 until we arrive at size 16×1616\times 16. This step is done at zero pseudo-temperature and without reintializing the parameters of the RNN. This idea was already proposed in the literature in Ref. [14]. The latter takes advantage of the translation invariance property encoded in the weight-sharing of the parameters of the RNN (see Eqs. 1, 2 and 3). The results in Fig. 3(b) show that for system sizes larger than 14×1414\times 14, the variational energy obtained by our RNN ansatz is more accurate compared to the energy obtained by DMRG. Interestingly, our RNN ansatz uses less than 0.1%0.1\% of the parameters of DMRG for system sizes larger than 14×1414\times 14.

Conclusion

In this paper, we have applied a modified variant of the two dimensional RNN wave function [1, 25] for the task of finding the ground state of the 2D Heisenberg model on the square and the triangular lattice. We have shown that applying symmetry and annealing helps to obtain highly accurate ground states. We have also demonstrated the power of our ansatz compared to DMRG for large system sizes on the triangular lattice, where frustration makes the problem more challenging. We believe that more advanced versions of RNN wave functions along with the idea of applying symmetries and annealing can make our ansatz a highly competitive tool for studying quantum many-body systems.

Note: The hyperparameters used to produce the results of this paper are detailed in Appendix. C. Furthermore, our reproducibility code can be found in Ref. [32].

Broader Impact

The scope of this paper is within quantum many-body physics, which aims to understand the behaviour of matter based on simple rules at the microscopic scale. In the best case, our method could enhance the state-of-the-art algorithms and enable a better understanding of unknown quantum systems.

Appendix A Two dimensional gated recurrent neural networks

In this section, we show how we incorporate the gating mechanism in our 2D cRNN wave function ansatz. The 2D RNN cell we use is based on the following recursion relations:

𝒉~i,j\displaystyle\bm{\tilde{h}}_{i,j} =tanh⁡([𝝈i−1,j;𝝈i,j−1]​T​[𝒉i−1,j;𝒉i,j−1]+𝒃),\displaystyle=\tanh\!\left([\bm{\sigma}_{i-1,j};\bm{\sigma}_{i,j-1}]T[\bm{h}_{i-1,j};\bm{h}_{i,j-1}]+\bm{b}\right), (6)
𝒖i,j\displaystyle\bm{u}_{i,j} =sigmoid​([𝝈i−1,j;𝝈i,j−1]​Tg​[𝒉i−1,j;𝒉i,j−1]+𝒃𝒈),\displaystyle=\text{sigmoid}\!\left([\bm{\sigma}_{i-1,j};\bm{\sigma}_{i,j-1}]T_{g}[\bm{h}_{i-1,j};\bm{h}_{i,j-1}]+\bm{b_{g}}\right), (7)
𝒉i,j\displaystyle\bm{h}_{i,j} =𝒖i,j⊙𝒉~i,j+(1−𝒖i,j)⊙(W⁡[𝒉i−1,j;𝒉i,j−1]).\displaystyle=\bm{u}_{i,j}\odot\bm{\tilde{h}}_{i,j}+(1-\bm{u}_{i,j})\odot(W[\bm{h}_{i-1,j};\bm{h}_{i,j-1}]). (8)

Here we obtain the state 𝒉i,j\bm{h}_{i,j} through a combination of the neighbouring hidden states 𝒉i−1,j,𝒉i,j−1\bm{h}_{i-1,j},\bm{h}_{i,j-1} and the candidate hidden state 𝒉~i,j\bm{\tilde{h}}_{i,j}. The update gate 𝒖i,j\bm{u}_{i,j} decides how much the candidate hidden state 𝒉~i,j\bm{\tilde{h}}_{i,j} will be modified. The latter combination allows to circumvent some of the limitations related to the vanishing gradient problem [35, 36]. Note that the size of the hidden state 𝒉i,j\bm{h}_{i,j} that we denote as dhd_{h} is a hyperparameter that we choose before optimizing the parameters of our ansatz. The tensors T,TgT,T_{g}, the weight matrix WW and the biases b,bgb,b_{g} are variational parameters of our RNN ansatz in addition to the parameters in Eqs. (2) and (3).

To show the advantage of a 2D gated RNN over the 2D non-gated RNN, we train them using the VMC scheme to find the ground state of the Heisenberg model on the square lattice with size 6×66\times 6. We find that the gated RNN allows to obtain a more accurate energy. More specifically, we plot the energy variance per spin σ2=(⟨H^2⟩−⟨H^⟩)2/N\sigma^{2}=(\langle\hat{H}^{2}\rangle-\langle\hat{H}\rangle)^{2}/N in Fig. 4(a). This quantity is a good indicator for the proximity of the ansatz to the ground state provided that local minima are avoided [37, 38, 39]. We observe that the gated RNN can get about an order of magnitude lower σ2\sigma^{2} compared to the non-gated RNN. The latter results demonstrate the advantage of adding the gating mechanism to our wave function ansatz.

Appendix B Annealing on the square lattice

In the results section, we have used T0=0T_{0}=0 on the square lattice which is equivalent to not doing annealing. The latter is motivated by the observation that the Heisenberg model on the square lattice is not frustrated and can be made stoquastic using the Marshall sign rule [29, 30]. To further corroborate this observation, we compare VMC with and without annealing on the square lattice for a system size 4×44\times 4 and report our results in Fig. 4(b). The latter illustrates that annealing does not show an advantage for large NannealingN_{\rm annealing} as opposed to the case of the triangular lattice demonstrated in Fig. 3(a). This result suggests that in the absence of frustration, there is no need to supplement VMC with annealing.

Appendix C Hyperparameters

In this section, we summarize the hyperparameters used to produce the main results of this paper in Tab. 1. We note that the training of our ansatz was performed using P100 GPUs.

In order to produce the results of Fig. 3(b), we use dh=300d_{h}=300 and Ns=100N_{s}=100 samples for training. We have first performed annealing on the system size 6×66\times 6 with Nwarmup=1000N_{\rm warmup}=1000 and Nannealing=10000N_{\rm annealing}=10000 and an initial pseudo-temperature T0=0.25T_{0}=0.25, while using a fixed learning rate η=5×10−4\eta=5\times 10^{-4}. In this initial phase, we only apply the U⁡(1)U(1) symmetry. In the next phase, we perform an additional 2500025000 gradients steps at zero pseudo-temperature and add an additional 2500025000 gradients steps after applying C2​dC_{2d} symmetry. The idea of adding more symmetries during training has been put forward in Ref. [20]. During this convergence phase, the learning rate is decayed as η=5×10−5/(1+t/2000)\eta=5\times 10^{-5}/(1+t/2000), where tt corresponds to the current number of convergence steps. We then increase the system size to 8×88\times 8, while keeping our ansatz parameters fixed, applying C2​dC_{2d} symmetry and while using zero pseudo-temperature. In this phase, the learning rate is fixed to η=10−5\eta=10^{-5}. After this step, we train our RNN ansatz until convergence. We repeat the same procedure for system sizes 10×1010\times 10, 12×1212\times 12, 14×1414\times 14 and 16×1616\times 16. We note that for 8×88\times 8, we add 4000040000 gradient steps. For 10×1010\times 10, we continue training with 2000020000 gradient steps. For 12×1212\times 12, we converge using 1000010000 training steps. For 14×1414\times 14, we continue training with 50005000 gradient steps. Finally, for 16×1616\times 16 we add 20002000 convergence steps.

To produce the DMRG results in Fig. 3(b), we used a bond dimension D=4000D=4000 for sizes 6×66\times 6, 8×88\times 8 and 10×1010\times 10. For 12×1212\times 12, we used D=3000D=3000 and for the sizes 14×1414\times 14 and 16×1616\times 16, we used D=2000D=2000 since we were not able to obtain the DMRG energy at D=4000D=4000 within a limit of 100100 GB memory allocation. The DMRG calculations were run using ITensor [41].

We finally note that the Marshall sign [29, 30] is applied on top of our cRNN wave function on the square lattice and on the triangular lattice during all our numerical experiments to speed up convergence. For DMRG, we observed that applying the Marshall sign does not affect the accuracy.

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.

Have a free development cycle? Help support accessibility at arXiv! Our collaborators at LaTeXML maintain a list of packages that need conversion, and welcome developer contributions.
